questions.question: Of the eight planets, one is closest to the Sun and zips around it in just 88 Earth days. Which planet is it?
questions.answer: Mercury, the smallest and fastest planet
choices: Mercury, the smallest and fastest planet
Mars, the rusty fourth planet
Pluto, no longer a true planet
Saturn, the ringed sixth planet
questions.context: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun. It has almost no atmosphere, so daytime can be over 400 C and night below -170 C. It zips around the Sun in 88 Earth days. Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.

questions.question: One planet has a giant red storm bigger than Earth that has been swirling for hundreds of years. Which one?
questions.answer: Jupiter, the biggest planet of all
choices: Jupiter, the biggest planet of all
Venus, the cloudy second planet
Saturn, the ringed sixth planet
Mars, the rusty red planet
questions.context: Jupiter is the largest planet in our solar system. The Great Red Spot is a storm observed since at least the 1830s, possibly since 1665. Jupiter has at least 95 known moons.

questions.question: One planet is famous for its bright icy rings — billions of chunks of frozen water and rock. Which planet?
questions.answer: Saturn, with its big bright rings
choices: Saturn, with its big bright rings
Mars, with its rusty red dust
Uranus, the tilted ice planet
Mercury, the closest to the Sun
questions.context: Saturn's rings were first seen by Galileo in 1610, though he didn't know what they were. They are made of countless ice and rock pieces, from dust-sized to house-sized.

questions.question: One planet is COVERED in volcanoes and is the hottest in our solar system (yes, hotter than Mercury). Which one?
questions.answer: Venus, hotter than Mercury
choices: Venus, hotter than Mercury
Mars, the rusty fourth planet
Saturn, the ringed planet
Neptune, the windy blue planet
questions.context: Venus has a thick carbon dioxide atmosphere that traps heat — surface temperatures reach about 465 C, hotter than Mercury despite being farther from the Sun. Surface pressure is 90 times Earth's.

questions.question: One planet is nicknamed the 'red planet' because of rusty iron in its dust, and has the tallest volcano in our system. Which?
questions.answer: Mars, home of Olympus Mons
choices: Mars, home of Olympus Mons
Mercury, the smallest planet
Jupiter, the biggest planet
Pluto, the dwarf planet
questions.context: Mars looks red because iron in its dust has rusted. Olympus Mons is about 22 km tall, almost three times the height of Mount Everest. Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos.

questions.question: From the Sun the planets go: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, then a giant. Which giant comes fifth?
questions.answer: Jupiter, the fifth from the Sun
choices: Jupiter, the fifth from the Sun
Saturn, the sixth from the Sun
Uranus, the seventh from the Sun
Neptune, the eighth from the Sun
questions.context: Order: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. One mnemonic: 'My Very Excellent Mother Just Served Us Nachos.' Jupiter is so big you could fit all the other planets inside it.

questions.question: The farthest official planet from the Sun is deep blue, very cold, and takes about 165 Earth years to go around once. Which planet?
questions.answer: Neptune, the eighth and last planet
choices: Neptune, the eighth and last planet
Jupiter, the largest planet
Uranus, the tilted planet
Mercury, the closest planet
questions.context: Neptune is the farthest of the eight planets. It is a deep blue from methane in its atmosphere and has the fastest winds in the solar system, over 2,000 km per hour.

questions.question: For 76 years kids learned about 9 planets. In 2006 astronomers voted to call Pluto something else. What did they call it?
questions.answer: A dwarf planet, not a true planet
choices: A dwarf planet, not a true planet
A giant asteroid lost in space
A frozen comet shaped like a ball
A captured moon of Neptune
questions.context: Pluto was discovered by Clyde Tombaugh in 1930 and called the ninth planet until 2006. The International Astronomical Union voted to reclassify it as a 'dwarf planet' because it shares its orbital zone with other icy bodies.

questions.question: When the Moon is between Earth and the Sun, its lit side faces away. What phase is that?
questions.answer: New moon, looking invisible from Earth
choices: New moon, looking invisible from Earth
Full moon, with the whole face lit
Half moon, with half lit and half dark
Blood moon, glowing reddish in space
questions.context: A new moon happens when the Moon sits between Earth and the Sun, so the lit side faces away from us. The Moon cycles through phases about every 29.5 days.

questions.question: When Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, sunlight bounces off the Moon's whole face. What phase is that?
questions.answer: Full moon, with the whole face lit up
choices: Full moon, with the whole face lit up
New moon, looking invisible from Earth
Quarter moon, with one quarter dark
Crescent moon, shaped like a sliver
questions.context: A full moon happens when Earth sits between the Sun and Moon. There is usually one full moon each month. Two full moons in one month is sometimes called a 'blue moon.'

questions.question: The Moon SEEMS to change shape over 29 days. Why does it look like that?
questions.answer: The Sun lights different parts as it orbits
choices: The Sun lights different parts as it orbits
Earth's shadow covers it for the whole month
The Moon really shrinks and then regrows
Space clouds slowly cover parts of it
questions.context: The Moon doesn't change shape — only how much of its lit side faces us. As the Moon orbits Earth, the angle between Sun, Moon, and Earth changes, so we see different fractions of the lit half.

questions.question: Sometimes the Moon passes exactly between Earth and the Sun, and the sky goes dark in the middle of the day. What is that called?
questions.answer: A total solar eclipse
choices: A total solar eclipse
A long lunar eclipse
A bright meteor shower
A glowing blue moon
questions.context: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon blocks the Sun's light from reaching part of Earth. Total solar eclipses are rare in any one spot. Never look at the Sun directly without eclipse glasses.

questions.question: Sometimes Earth passes between the Sun and the full Moon, casting a shadow that turns the Moon dim or reddish. What is that called?
questions.answer: A lunar eclipse, or blood moon
choices: A lunar eclipse, or blood moon
A bright solar eclipse
A nighttime shooting star
A glowing super moon
questions.context: A lunar eclipse happens during a full moon when Earth lines up between the Sun and Moon. The Moon often turns rusty red because Earth's atmosphere bends red light onto it. Lunar eclipses are safe to view.

questions.question: Why is it never safe to stare at the Sun during a solar eclipse without proper glasses?
questions.answer: Even a sliver of Sun can burn your eyes
choices: Even a sliver of Sun can burn your eyes
The Moon gives off a rare harmful ray
Eclipse light has been shown to itch skin
The sky goes too dark for human eyes
questions.context: Even when most of the Sun is covered, the visible edge is bright enough to damage the retina. The retina has no pain sensors, so the burn happens silently. Eclipse glasses block about 99.999% of sunlight.

questions.question: Why does Earth have summer and winter at all?
questions.answer: Earth is tilted toward or away from the Sun
choices: Earth is tilted toward or away from the Sun
Earth moves closer in summer, farther in winter
The Sun burns hotter for half the year
Space wind pushes Earth back and forth
questions.context: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees. As Earth orbits, different halves get more direct sunlight at different times. Earth is actually CLOSEST to the Sun in January (Northern winter), so distance isn't the cause.

questions.question: When it is summer in Florida, what season is it down in Argentina (south of the equator)?
questions.answer: Winter, the opposite of Florida
choices: Winter, the opposite of Florida
Summer, the same as Florida
Spring, just before their summer
Autumn, just after their summer
questions.context: When the Northern Hemisphere is tilted TOWARD the Sun (June-August), the Southern Hemisphere is tilted AWAY — so it's winter there. Christmas in Argentina or Australia happens in summer.

questions.question: Twice a year, around March 20 and September 22, day and night are nearly equal everywhere. What is that day called?
questions.answer: An equinox, meaning 'equal night'
choices: An equinox, meaning 'equal night'
A solstice, when sun 'stands still'
An eclipse, when the Sun is dim
A meridian, when noon goes long
questions.context: Equinox means 'equal night' in Latin. On the equinoxes the Sun shines straight down on the equator. The two solstices (around June 21 and December 21) are the longest and shortest days of the year.

questions.question: Earth turns all the way around once each day, giving us day and night. About how long does one full spin take?
questions.answer: About 24 hours, our day-night cycle
choices: About 24 hours, our day-night cycle
About 12 hours, only the day part
About 7 days, a full week of spin
About 30 days, the same as the moon
questions.context: Earth spins on its axis once every 24 hours, which is why we have day and night. Strictly, one spin relative to the stars is 23 hours 56 minutes; the extra 4 minutes is because Earth has also moved around the Sun.

questions.question: When it is noon in New York and the Sun is high overhead, what is it in Tokyo, across the world?
questions.answer: The dark middle of the night
choices: The dark middle of the night
Also bright noon, with sun high
Sunrise, with the Sun just up
Sunset, with the Sun just down
questions.context: Tokyo is about halfway around the world from New York. When one side of Earth faces the Sun, the other side is dark. Time zones exist because the same instant looks different all around the globe.

questions.question: Hot melted rock cools and hardens. What KIND of rock is made that way? (Granite and obsidian count.)
questions.answer: Igneous rock, from cooled magma
choices: Igneous rock, from cooled magma
Sedimentary rock, from layers of mud
Metamorphic rock, changed by heat
Crystal rock, from frozen sand
questions.context: 'Igneous' comes from the Latin word for fire ('ignis'). When magma cools slowly underground, it forms rocks like granite. When lava cools quickly on the surface, it forms rocks like obsidian and basalt.

questions.question: Sand, mud, and shells settle in rivers and oceans, layer on layer, and slowly harden into rock. What kind of rock is that?
questions.answer: Sedimentary rock, from settled layers
choices: Sedimentary rock, from settled layers
Igneous rock, from cooled magma
Metamorphic rock, changed by heat
Lava rock, from a recent eruption
questions.context: Sedimentary rocks (sandstone, limestone, shale) form from squeezed-and-cemented layers of sand, mud, and shells. Most fossils are found in sedimentary rocks. The Grand Canyon shows the layers beautifully.

questions.question: Take any rock and squish-and-heat it deep underground for a long time. What kind of rock results? (Marble and slate count.)
questions.answer: Metamorphic rock, meaning 'changed form'
choices: Metamorphic rock, meaning 'changed form'
Igneous rock, from cooled magma
Sedimentary rock, from layers
Mineral rock, made of one crystal
questions.context: 'Metamorphic' means 'changed form.' Marble starts as limestone, then heat and pressure recrystallize it. Slate starts as shale. The three rock types form the rock cycle.

questions.question: Igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic — these rock types can SLOWLY change into each other over millions of years. What is that called?
questions.answer: The rock cycle, slow but never stopping
choices: The rock cycle, slow but never stopping
The water cycle, with rain and ocean
The food chain, with eaters and eaten
The carbon ladder, with energy steps
questions.context: The rock cycle: an igneous rock can be worn down into sediment, buried into sedimentary rock, then heated into metamorphic rock, then melted back into magma. It takes millions of years but never stops.

questions.question: Melted rock inside the Earth is called magma. What is the SAME melted rock called once it comes OUT of a volcano?
questions.answer: Lava, magma above the surface
choices: Lava, magma above the surface
Still magma, just hotter than before
Tar, a black sticky kind of rock
Ash, the powder left over after
questions.context: Magma is melted rock UNDERGROUND. The same stuff becomes lava once it reaches the surface. Lava can be over 1,000 C. As it cools, it hardens into igneous rock like basalt.

questions.question: In 79 AD a Roman city was buried under ash from Mount Vesuvius, including bread still in ovens. What was that city?
questions.answer: Pompeii, buried by Mount Vesuvius
choices: Pompeii, buried by Mount Vesuvius
Atlantis, the lost ocean city
Sparta, in ancient Greek lands
Carthage, in northern Africa
questions.context: Mount Vesuvius erupted on August 24, 79 AD, burying Pompeii and Herculaneum under meters of ash and pumice. Archaeologists later found preserved homes, paintings, loaves of bread, and the shapes of people. Vesuvius is still active.

questions.question: Hawaii was built entirely by volcanoes. The biggest volcano on Earth (from its base on the seafloor) sits there. Which island chain?
questions.answer: Hawaii, with Mauna Loa as its giant
choices: Hawaii, with Mauna Loa as its giant
Iceland, with many small volcanoes
Japan, with Mount Fuji nearby
Sicily, with Mount Etna nearby
questions.context: Mauna Loa on Hawaii's Big Island rises about 9 km from the seafloor — taller than Mount Everest if measured from the base. The Hawaiian islands sit over a 'hotspot' in Earth's mantle that has been making volcanoes for millions of years.

questions.question: Earth's crust is split into giant plates that slowly bump and slide. The shaking we feel when they slip is called what?
questions.answer: An earthquake, from slipping plates
choices: An earthquake, from slipping plates
A volcano, from rising magma
A tornado, from spinning wind
An avalanche, from sliding snow
questions.context: Earth's surface is broken into about 15 large plates that move a few centimeters a year. At faults, plates can stick and then suddenly slip, releasing energy as an earthquake. California's San Andreas Fault is famous.

questions.question: Scientists use a seismograph to measure earthquakes. The number it gives tells you what about each one?
questions.answer: How much energy the quake released
choices: How much energy the quake released
How many people felt the quake
How many minutes the quake lasted
How deep below ground it started
questions.context: The Richter scale (1935) and the moment magnitude scale rate quake strength. Each step up is about 32 times more energy: a magnitude 7 releases 32 times more energy than a magnitude 6.

questions.question: When a big underwater earthquake shoves up the seafloor, what huge wave can race outward and crash onto far coastlines?
questions.answer: A tsunami, named the 'harbor wave'
choices: A tsunami, named the 'harbor wave'
A typhoon, a spinning Pacific storm
A whirlpool, a spinning small drain
A geyser, a hot water spout on land
questions.context: 'Tsunami' is Japanese for 'harbor wave.' A tsunami crosses the deep ocean as fast as a jet plane (up to 800 km/h). The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami killed about 230,000 people across many countries.

questions.question: On a hot day, water from a puddle quietly disappears into the air. What is that step of the water cycle called?
questions.answer: Evaporation, water turning into vapor
choices: Evaporation, water turning into vapor
Condensation, vapor making clouds
Precipitation, rain falling back down
Filtration, water flowing through dirt
questions.context: The water cycle: evaporation, condensation (vapor forms clouds), precipitation, runoff back to rivers and oceans. The same water has been cycling on Earth for billions of years — rain you drink contains atoms dinosaurs once drank.

questions.question: After lightning flashes, you sometimes hear a loud rolling BOOM a few seconds later. What is that boom?
questions.answer: Thunder, the sound of heated air
choices: Thunder, the sound of heated air
Clouds bumping into each other
Wind hitting faraway mountains
The sound of rain in upper sky
questions.context: Lightning is hotter than the surface of the Sun — about 30,000 C. It heats the air so fast that the air explodes outward, creating thunder. Light travels faster than sound, so we see the flash first.

questions.question: A huge spinning storm over warm oceans is called a hurricane in America. What is the SAME kind of storm called in Asia?
questions.answer: A typhoon, the Asian name for it
choices: A typhoon, the Asian name for it
A tornado, the funnel-cloud storm
A blizzard, a heavy snowstorm
A monsoon, a rainy wind season
questions.context: Hurricanes (Atlantic + Eastern Pacific), typhoons (Western Pacific), and cyclones (Indian Ocean + Southern Hemisphere) are all the same kind of storm — just different regional names. They form over warm ocean water.

questions.question: A tornado is a fast-spinning funnel of wind that touches the ground. Which US region gets the MOST tornadoes?
questions.answer: The central plains, called Tornado Alley
choices: The central plains, called Tornado Alley
The northeast, mostly New England
The far west, by the Pacific Ocean
The far north, including Alaska
questions.context: Tornado Alley roughly covers Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, Nebraska, and nearby states. Warm wet air from the Gulf crashing into cool dry air from the Rockies sets up the storm conditions. The US gets about 1,200 tornadoes a year.

questions.question: More than two-thirds of Earth is covered by salty water. Which single ocean is the BIGGEST?
questions.answer: The Pacific, bigger than all dry land
choices: The Pacific, bigger than all dry land
The Atlantic, between the Americas
The Indian, south of southern Asia
The Arctic, surrounding the North Pole
questions.context: The Pacific covers about 165 million square kilometers — roughly 30% of Earth's surface, more than all the land on the planet. Ferdinand Magellan named it 'Pacifico' (peaceful) in 1521 because his ships had calm weather crossing it.

questions.question: Mount Everest could SINK into the deepest spot on Earth with over a kilometer of water still on top. Where is that deep spot?
questions.answer: The Mariana Trench, in the Pacific
choices: The Mariana Trench, in the Pacific
The Bermuda Triangle, off Florida
The Great Barrier Reef, off Australia
The Sargasso Sea, by Bermuda
questions.context: The Mariana Trench in the western Pacific reaches about 11,000 m below sea level at its deepest point, Challenger Deep. Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh first reached the bottom in 1960 in the bathyscaphe Trieste.

questions.question: Ocean water is salty. Where did all that salt first come from?
questions.answer: Rain slowly washed it from rocks
choices: Rain slowly washed it from rocks
Humans put it there to keep ice off
Sea creatures squirted it for defense
Lightning split sea water into salt
questions.context: When rain falls on land, it dissolves tiny bits of salt from rocks. Rivers carry the salt to the sea. Water evaporates from the ocean leaving the salt behind. After billions of years, oceans are about 3.5% salt.

questions.question: Fluffy white clouds look like cotton, but they are not cotton. What are clouds REALLY made of?
questions.answer: Tiny droplets of water (or ice)
choices: Tiny droplets of water (or ice)
Smoke from chimneys and fires
Bits of salt from ocean wind
Tiny pieces of plant pollen
questions.context: Clouds form when water vapor in warm rising air cools and condenses on tiny dust particles. Each droplet is far smaller than a raindrop. A typical cloud weighs as much as a million pounds, but each droplet is so tiny it stays up.

questions.question: Big puffy white clouds with flat bottoms — the cotton-ball kind on a sunny day — have a special name. Which?
questions.answer: Cumulus clouds, from Latin for 'heap'
choices: Cumulus clouds, from Latin for 'heap'
Cirrus clouds, from Latin for 'curl'
Stratus clouds, from Latin for 'layer'
Nimbus clouds, from Latin for 'rain'
questions.context: 'Cumulus' is Latin for 'heap.' Cumulus clouds form on warm sunny days when rising air carries moisture upward. If they grow tall and dark, they become cumulonimbus — the storm clouds.

questions.question: Thin wispy clouds high up that look like horse tails or feathers are made mostly of tiny ICE crystals. What are they called?
questions.answer: Cirrus clouds, way up high and icy
choices: Cirrus clouds, way up high and icy
Cumulus clouds, puffy and low
Stratus clouds, in flat gray sheets
Fog clouds, hugging the ground
questions.context: 'Cirrus' comes from Latin for 'curl of hair.' Cirrus clouds form above 6,000 m where the air is below freezing, so they are made of ice. Lots of cirrus from the west often means a weather front and rain are on the way.

questions.question: Earth's crust is broken into giant plates that crash and crumple over millions of years. What does that crumpling MAKE?
questions.answer: Mountains, slowly rising from crashes
choices: Mountains, slowly rising from crashes
Oceans, big basins between plates
Deserts, with little rain or trees
Glaciers, with ice that flows slowly
questions.context: The Himalayas (including Mount Everest) are still rising today because India is crashing into Asia at about 5 cm per year. The Andes, Alps, and Rockies were all formed by colliding tectonic plates.

questions.question: The tallest mountain in the world (measured from sea level) sits on the border of Nepal and Tibet. What is it called?
questions.answer: Mount Everest, on the Nepal border
choices: Mount Everest, on the Nepal border
Mount Kilimanjaro, in east Africa
Mount Fuji, in Japan's main island
Denali, in the state of Alaska
questions.context: Mount Everest is about 8,849 m tall and still rising slowly. It is named after George Everest, a British surveyor. The Nepali name is Sagarmatha and the Tibetan is Chomolungma. Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay first reached the summit in 1953.

questions.question: Inside the Sun, hydrogen atoms slam together and turn into helium, releasing HUGE energy. What is that process called?
questions.answer: Nuclear fusion, smashing atoms together
choices: Nuclear fusion, smashing atoms together
Nuclear fission, splitting atoms apart
Burning oxygen, like a candle flame
Electric sparking, between two wires
questions.context: The Sun has been fusing hydrogen into helium for about 4.6 billion years and has roughly 5 billion years of fuel left. Fusion needs immense heat — about 15 million C at the Sun's core. The Sun isn't 'burning' chemically; it's a nuclear reactor.

questions.question: Why does the Moon shine in the night sky if it isn't a star?
questions.answer: It reflects sunlight back to Earth
choices: It reflects sunlight back to Earth
Its hot core glows from the inside
Distant stars combine to light it
It produces its own moonlight
questions.context: The Moon, Mars, Jupiter, and Venus all look bright because they reflect sunlight. None make their own light. Only stars (huge balls of fusing hydrogen) shine on their own. The Sun is the closest star to us.

questions.question: Sunlight takes some time to travel through space. About how long is sunlight on its way to Earth?
questions.answer: About 8 minutes from Sun to Earth
choices: About 8 minutes from Sun to Earth
About 8 seconds from Sun to Earth
About 8 hours from Sun to Earth
Almost instantly, less than one tick
questions.context: Earth is about 150 million km from the Sun, and light travels about 300,000 km per second. The light hitting your face right now LEFT the Sun about 8 minutes ago. Light from the next-closest star (Proxima Centauri) takes about 4.2 years.

questions.question: The Sun is huge compared to Earth. About how many Earths could fit INSIDE the Sun?
questions.answer: About one million tiny Earths
choices: About one million tiny Earths
About one hundred tiny Earths
About one thousand tiny Earths
About ten billion tiny Earths
questions.context: The Sun's diameter is about 1.4 million km — roughly 109 times Earth's. By volume, you could fit about 1.3 million Earths inside the Sun. The Sun holds about 99.8% of the entire mass of our solar system.

questions.question: Earth has a thin outer crust, a hot squishy middle, and a very hot center ball. What is the very HOTTEST middle ball called?
questions.answer: The core, with melted iron inside
choices: The core, with melted iron inside
The mantle, the slow-flowing layer
The crust, the thin outer rocky skin
The atmosphere, all the layers of air
questions.context: Earth's layers: crust (rocky, thin), mantle (hot rock flowing slowly), outer core (liquid iron and nickel), inner core (solid iron and nickel, about 5,400 C). The swirling liquid core makes Earth's magnetic field.

questions.question: Compass needles all point the same way no matter where you stand. What invisible thing pulls them?
questions.answer: Earth's own magnetic field
choices: Earth's own magnetic field
Plain gravity toward the Sun
Wind currents in the upper sky
Static from rubbing in the clouds
questions.context: Earth acts like a giant magnet, with a north and south magnetic pole. The field is made by churning liquid iron in Earth's outer core. It also protects us from harmful solar particles, and creates the northern lights (aurora).

questions.question: Astronauts on the Moon could jump much HIGHER than on Earth. Why?
questions.answer: The Moon's gravity is much weaker
choices: The Moon's gravity is much weaker
The Moon has no air to push against
Astronauts wore very light moon boots
Time runs faster on the Moon than Earth
questions.context: The Moon has about 1/6 of Earth's gravity because it has much less mass. An 80 kg Earth astronaut feels only 13 kg there. Apollo astronauts famously hopped instead of walked. Twelve people have walked on the Moon (1969-1972).

questions.question: On the ocean, people watching a ship sail far away see it disappear BOTTOM FIRST below the horizon. What does that show?
questions.answer: Earth is a sphere, not a flat disk
choices: Earth is a sphere, not a flat disk
Ships shrink as they go far away
The sea slowly pulls ships under
Light can't travel across oceans
questions.context: Ancient Greek thinkers like Eratosthenes (around 240 BC) figured out Earth was round and measured its size well using shadows. Ships disappearing hull-first, the round shadow Earth casts on the Moon during eclipses, and photos from space all confirm it.

questions.question: Earth's air is a mix of gases. Which gas is the MAIN one — the most common in every breath?
questions.answer: Nitrogen, about 78% of the air
choices: Nitrogen, about 78% of the air
Oxygen, about 21% of the air
Carbon dioxide, the gas plants use
Helium, the light gas in balloons
questions.context: Earth's atmosphere is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and 1% other gases. Many kids guess oxygen because we breathe it, but oxygen is only the second most common gas. Plants need carbon dioxide; animals need oxygen.

questions.question: In 1610 Galileo pointed a new telescope at Jupiter and saw four little dots moving around it night after night. What had he just found?
questions.answer: Jupiter has its own four small worlds
choices: Jupiter has its own four small worlds
Jupiter is much hotter than the Sun
Jupiter is a closer star than our Sun
Jupiter is made of solid clear ice
questions.context: Galileo Galilei saw Jupiter's four largest moons in January 1610: Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto. They are still called the 'Galilean moons.' Moons going around Jupiter showed Earth was NOT the center of everything.

questions.question: Galileo's telescope showed the Moon's surface was not smooth and perfect at all. What did he actually see up there?
questions.answer: Mountains and craters on a rocky moon
choices: Mountains and craters on a rocky moon
Cities of light made by moon people
A smooth shiny ball as taught for ages
A flat painted picture in the sky
questions.context: Galileo published his telescope discoveries in 'Starry Messenger' (1610). Until then, the Moon was thought to be a perfect smooth sphere. Galileo even estimated mountain heights from shadows. He also found the Sun has spots.

questions.question: A story says Galileo dropped a heavy ball and a light ball off the Leaning Tower of Pisa. What did he say happens?
questions.answer: They land at about the same time
choices: They land at about the same time
The heavy ball hits MUCH sooner
The light ball hits MUCH sooner
Both float and never hit at all
questions.context: The Tower of Pisa story may be legend, but the idea is real: without air, all objects fall at the same rate. An Apollo 15 astronaut dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon in 1971 to prove it. Galileo's claim went against 2,000 years of Aristotle's teaching.

questions.question: Galileo said Earth goes around the Sun, not the other way. In 1633 the Church was very upset. What happened to him?
questions.answer: He was made to take it back and stay home
choices: He was made to take it back and stay home
He got a big medal and a parade in Rome
He was ignored politely for centuries
His idea was adopted within a month
questions.context: Galileo's 'Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems' (1632) defended the Sun-centered view of Copernicus. He was tried by the Inquisition in 1633 and forced to recant. He spent his last years under house arrest. The Church formally apologized for the case in 1992.

questions.question: Galileo was an outsider who turned out RIGHT but experts mocked him. What's the lesson kids learn from his story?
questions.answer: Even big experts can be wrong for a while
choices: Even big experts can be wrong for a while
Outsiders are always wrong about nature
Books should never be checked by readers
Scientists always agree on everything
questions.context: Galileo's case is one of the most famous in science history — a single outsider with better evidence held to the truth against powerful institutions. The story repeats: Semmelweis, Wegener, Marshall, all rejected then vindicated.

questions.question: A famous legend says young Isaac Newton was under a tree when something fell and sparked a big idea. What fell?
questions.answer: An apple, says the famous story
choices: An apple, says the famous story
A pear, just before lunchtime
A coconut, on a hot summer day
A book of poetry, says one tale
questions.context: The apple story comes from Newton himself, told to friends late in life. The real question wasn't 'why did the apple fall?' but 'why does the apple fall DOWN but the Moon stays UP?' Newton's answer: same gravity pulls on both — the Moon is moving sideways fast enough to keep missing the Earth.

questions.question: Newton said the same invisible PULL that makes apples fall ALSO keeps the Moon in orbit. What did he call this pull?
questions.answer: Gravity, the universal pull
choices: Gravity, the universal pull
Magnetism, the iron-pulling force
Friction, what slows sliding things
Electricity, the spark in wires
questions.context: Newton's law of universal gravitation (1687) was the first to say the same force works everywhere — on apples, the Moon, planets, stars. The math worked so well it predicted comets and planets we hadn't seen yet.

questions.question: Newton's third law: for every action, an equal and opposite reaction. If you push a wall hard, what does it do?
questions.answer: It pushes back with the same force
choices: It pushes back with the same force
It absorbs the push and gives none back
Only soft walls push back, not hard ones
It moves a tiny bit forward over time
questions.context: Newton's third law is why rockets work — burning fuel pushes gases OUT the back, and the gases push the rocket FORWARD. It is also why ice skaters slide backward when they push each other. Newton's three laws of motion are still used by engineers today.

questions.question: Newton put sunlight through a glass prism and saw a rainbow appear on the wall. What did that prove?
questions.answer: White sunlight is many colors mixed
choices: White sunlight is many colors mixed
Prisms add colors that weren't there
Sunlight is one pure color throughout
Rainbows are painted on the prism
questions.context: Newton's prism experiments (around 1666) showed white light contains all rainbow colors: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. Rainbows in the sky work the same way: raindrops act like little prisms.

questions.question: In 1831 a young Charles Darwin sailed around the world for almost 5 years as the naturalist on a British ship. What ship?
questions.answer: HMS Beagle, on a five-year voyage
choices: HMS Beagle, on a five-year voyage
HMS Victory, Nelson's old warship
HMS Titanic, a doomed ocean liner
HMS Endeavour, Captain Cook's ship
questions.context: Darwin was 22 when he joined HMS Beagle in 1831. The voyage took him to South America, the Galapagos, Australia, and around Africa. He collected fossils, plants, animals, and most importantly his observations of how species differed between places.

questions.question: On a group of islands far off South America, Darwin saw small birds — each island had birds with slightly different beaks. What birds?
questions.answer: Galapagos finches, with varied beaks
choices: Galapagos finches, with varied beaks
Penguins, sliding on the icy shore
Albatrosses, with huge wide wings
Parrots, bright green in the trees
questions.context: Darwin's Galapagos finches (about 15 species) became the textbook example of how species can change to fit their environment. Bigger beaks could crack tough seeds; pointier beaks could eat insects. One ancestor must have arrived and slowly split into many species.

questions.question: Darwin's big idea: animals with helpful traits live to have more babies, who also have those traits. What did he call this?
questions.answer: Natural selection, over many generations
choices: Natural selection, over many generations
Spontaneous generation, life from non-life
Sudden creation, all at once
Random shuffling, no real pattern
questions.context: Natural selection: in any group, some individuals have traits that help them survive and reproduce better. Over many generations, those traits become more common. Darwin's 'On the Origin of Species' (1859) laid out the theory with mountains of evidence.

questions.question: Darwin waited about 20 years to publish his big idea — he worried it would upset people. WHY would it upset them?
questions.answer: It says all living things share ancestors
choices: It says all living things share ancestors
It says scientists should never test ideas
It says Earth is much younger than it looks
It says animals should not be studied
questions.context: Darwin gathered evidence for two decades before publishing in 1859 — only then because Alfred Russel Wallace was about to publish similar ideas. The idea that humans share ancestors with apes — and ultimately all life — challenged many people's beliefs at the time and still does.

questions.question: Born in Poland, working in France, Marie Curie and husband Pierre found TWO new elements together. Which two?
questions.answer: Polonium and radium, two glowing elements
choices: Polonium and radium, two glowing elements
Helium and neon, two common bright gases
Gold and silver, two ancient shiny metals
Iron and copper, two daily-life metals
questions.context: Marie Curie named polonium (1898) after her homeland, Poland. She and Pierre discovered radium later that year. Both are 'radioactive' — slowly giving off energy. Pierre died in a street accident in 1906; Marie kept working and won a second Nobel in 1911.

questions.question: Marie Curie's 100-year-old lab notebooks are kept in special lead-lined boxes. Why are they so dangerous to touch?
questions.answer: They still give off radium radiation
choices: They still give off radium radiation
They are written in a secret unknown code
They are the only copies of a famous bomb plan
They are too valuable to ever open up
questions.context: Curie worked with radium without knowing how dangerous it was. Her notebooks (and even her cookbook) are still measurably radioactive — they will be for about another 1,500 years. She died in 1934 of a blood disease likely caused by all the radiation.

questions.question: Marie Curie is the only person ever to win Nobel Prizes in TWO different sciences. Which two sciences?
questions.answer: Physics and Chemistry, both Nobel-winning
choices: Physics and Chemistry, both Nobel-winning
Biology and Medicine, twice over
Astronomy and Geology, twice over
Math and Engineering, twice over
questions.context: Marie Curie won the 1903 Nobel in Physics (with Pierre and Henri Becquerel) for radioactivity, and the 1911 Nobel in Chemistry (alone) for polonium and radium. No one else has Nobels in two different sciences. Her daughter Irene also won a Nobel in Chemistry in 1935.

questions.question: During World War I, Marie Curie drove special vans right up to the front lines. What did the vans carry?
questions.answer: X-ray machines for wounded soldiers
choices: X-ray machines for wounded soldiers
Secret messages back to French command
Cooking gear for hot food in trenches
Bright lamps to keep soldiers brave at night
questions.context: Curie organized about 20 mobile X-ray vans known as 'petites Curies' (little Curies) during WWI. She trained women to operate them and drove them to the front herself. They helped surgeons treat over a million wounded soldiers.

questions.question: Marie Curie taught herself in a freezing Paris attic, topped her physics class, and won TWO Nobels. Today she is what?
questions.answer: One of the greatest scientists in history
choices: One of the greatest scientists in history
A factory worker who never went to school
A famous queen of a small country
A young athlete from the Olympic games
questions.context: When Curie arrived at the Sorbonne in 1891, women were rarely accepted in science. She had to fight for lab space, recognition, and even her second Nobel. Today, the element curium (Cm) is named after her and Pierre.

questions.question: Albert Einstein's tiny famous equation E=mc^2 says that a tiny bit of MASS can turn into a HUGE amount of what?
questions.answer: Energy, an enormous amount
choices: Energy, an enormous amount
Water, a useful clean liquid
Food, ready to be eaten
Air, the gas you breathe
questions.context: E=mc^2 says energy equals mass times the speed of light squared. Light's speed is a huge number, and squaring it makes it bigger still. So tiny mass becomes huge energy. This is the principle behind both nuclear power and nuclear bombs.

questions.question: Einstein liked 'thought experiments' — picturing strange situations in his mind. What did these help him do?
questions.answer: Think out how space, time, and light work
choices: Think out how space, time, and light work
Just take a peaceful break after lunch
Plan a real light-beam-riding bike one day
Teach little kids to ride small bicycles
questions.context: Einstein began the 'riding a light beam' thought experiment as a teenager. It led him eventually to special relativity (1905) — which said time and space themselves change for fast-moving observers. Many big physics ideas have started with carefully imagined situations.

questions.question: Einstein's theory of gravity (general relativity, 1915) said gravity is not really a pull at all. So what IS gravity?
questions.answer: A bending of space and time by mass
choices: A bending of space and time by mass
Invisible strings between two objects
A wind blowing down from above
A force pulling toward the equator
questions.context: Einstein's general relativity says heavy objects warp the fabric of space and time around them, like a heavy ball bending a stretched sheet. Things 'falling' are following the bend. Confirmed in 1919 when starlight was seen to bend around the Sun during a total eclipse.

questions.question: Einstein was offered the job of PRESIDENT of a country in 1952 — a great honor — but he politely turned it down. Which country?
questions.answer: Israel, just a few years old then
choices: Israel, just a few years old then
Germany, his old birth country
France, his neighbor in Europe
Italy, where Galileo had lived
questions.context: After Chaim Weizmann (Israel's first president) died in 1952, Einstein was offered the position. He declined, saying he was unsuited for politics and lacked the practical skills the job required. Einstein had fled Germany when the Nazis took power and became a US citizen in 1940.

questions.question: In the 1700s smallpox killed about 1 in 10 people. English doctor Edward Jenner noticed one group almost NEVER caught it. Who?
questions.answer: Milkmaids who had already had cowpox
choices: Milkmaids who had already had cowpox
Farmers who only ate root vegetables
Sailors who spent years out at sea
Bakers who handled bread all day
questions.context: Cowpox is a mild cousin of smallpox that milkmaids often caught from cows. Jenner noticed milkmaids who had survived cowpox almost never got smallpox. He had a hunch the milder disease was protecting them from the deadly one.

questions.question: Edward Jenner tested his cowpox idea in 1796 on an 8-year-old boy named James Phipps. What did he do exactly?
questions.answer: Gave him cowpox, then exposed him to smallpox
choices: Gave him cowpox, then exposed him to smallpox
Asked him to drink milk every day for a year
Sent him to live among cows for a week
Painted his skin nightly with a cream
questions.context: Jenner inoculated young Phipps with cowpox in May 1796. Weeks later he deliberately exposed him to smallpox — Phipps didn't get sick. By today's rules this would be banned, but it worked. Jenner had just invented the world's first vaccine.

questions.question: The word VACCINE comes from a Latin word. What does that Latin root word mean?
questions.answer: Cow, as in cowpox
choices: Cow, as in cowpox
Needle, like a sharp shot
Doctor, who gives the shot
Sleep, as in feeling tired
questions.context: Vaccine comes from 'vacca,' Latin for cow — because Edward Jenner's first vaccine used cowpox to protect people from smallpox. The word entered medicine through Jenner's work in the 1790s. Today we have vaccines for many diseases.

questions.question: Smallpox once killed hundreds of millions. In 1980 the World Health Organization said something amazing about it. What?
questions.answer: Smallpox had been wiped out on Earth
choices: Smallpox had been wiped out on Earth
Smallpox was twice as common worldwide
Smallpox had been given a new long name
Smallpox was a fictional made-up disease
questions.context: Smallpox is the ONLY human infectious disease ever fully wiped out. WHO declared eradication in May 1980, after a global vaccination campaign started in 1967. The last natural case was Ali Maow Maalin in Somalia in October 1977.

questions.question: In the 1940s and 50s, polio paralyzed thousands of US kids each summer. In 1955 a doctor announced a vaccine. Who was he?
questions.answer: Jonas Salk, the polio vaccine doctor
choices: Jonas Salk, the polio vaccine doctor
Edward Jenner, an old English doctor
Louis Pasteur, a famous French chemist
Alexander Fleming, the penicillin doctor
questions.context: Jonas Salk announced his polio vaccine on April 12, 1955. American cities held parades; church bells rang. Before it, polio struck about 50,000 American kids a year and left many in iron lungs. After widespread vaccination, US polio cases fell to almost zero by the early 1960s.

questions.question: TV asked Jonas Salk who owned the patent on his polio vaccine. What did he famously answer?
questions.answer: There was no patent; could you patent the Sun?
choices: There was no patent; could you patent the Sun?
His own family was set to own it for years
The US government quietly owned the rights
A secret company had bought all the rights
questions.context: Salk's famous reply came on a 1955 TV interview with Edward R. Murrow. He never patented his vaccine — he wanted it to reach as many children as possible. Economists later estimated the unpatented choice cost him around $7 billion. He stayed a working scientist all his life.

questions.question: Albert Sabin later made a different polio vaccine, given by mouth on a sugar cube. Why was that easier than a shot?
questions.answer: Kids could just swallow it anywhere
choices: Kids could just swallow it anywhere
It also worked the same day taken
It was made of regular kitchen sugar
It also cured the common cold quickly
questions.context: Albert Sabin's oral polio vaccine (1961) was easier to give than Salk's injected version, especially in places without trained medical staff. Kids could swallow a few drops on a sugar cube. The two vaccines together drove polio close to extinction worldwide.

questions.question: In Vienna in 1847, new mothers were dying of fever. Ignaz Semmelweis saw doctors going from corpses to babies. What did he tell them?
questions.answer: Wash hands in chlorine water first
choices: Wash hands in chlorine water first
Switch to wearing thick leather gloves
Stop all talking during the delivery
Pray for one hour before each birth
questions.context: Semmelweis figured out doctors were carrying invisible 'cadaverous particles' (germs) from autopsies to maternity wards. He had them wash with chlorinated lime. Deaths dropped from about 18% to about 1%. This was decades before anyone knew about germs.

questions.question: Semmelweis SHOWED with numbers that handwashing saved lives. How did most other doctors of his day react?
questions.answer: Mocked him; he was put in an asylum
choices: Mocked him; he was put in an asylum
All hospitals copied his rule in months
He won a great prize and named a hospital
Everyone in Europe adopted his idea fast
questions.context: Semmelweis's evidence was strong, but he couldn't EXPLAIN why handwashing worked (germ theory came later from Pasteur and Koch). Many doctors were offended by the idea they had been killing patients. He was institutionalized in 1865 and died there, possibly beaten by guards.

questions.question: Semmelweis was RIGHT but died unhonored. What's the warning in his story?
questions.answer: Being right is not the same as being believed
choices: Being right is not the same as being believed
Doctors always agree with new research
Old hospitals were perfectly safe places
Handwashing is a fairly minor habit
questions.context: The 'Semmelweis effect' is the name now used when people reject something that contradicts what they already believe. His story is sometimes paired with Wegener, Marshall, Mendel — all right, all rejected, all eventually vindicated.

questions.question: In a quiet monastery in the 1860s, Austrian monk Gregor Mendel carefully grew thousands of plants. What plant did he study?
questions.answer: Pea plants, about 28,000 of them
choices: Pea plants, about 28,000 of them
Apple trees, with red apples
Sunflowers, with bright yellow heads
Cabbage plants, in long green rows
questions.context: Mendel grew about 28,000 pea plants over 8 years in the garden of Saint Thomas' Abbey in Brno (now in the Czech Republic). He chose peas because they grow fast, breed predictably, and have clear features.

questions.question: Mendel crossed TALL and SHORT pea plants. All babies grew tall. But some GRANDCHILDREN were short. What did that show?
questions.answer: Traits can hide one round, then return
choices: Traits can hide one round, then return
Plants choose how tall to grow each year
Short plants always die before babies
Tall plants only marry tall plants
questions.context: Mendel discovered what we now call DOMINANT and RECESSIVE traits. Tall masks short, but the short instructions are still in the plant. About 1 in 4 grandchildren show the hidden short trait. This was the start of modern genetics.

questions.question: Mendel published his pea results in 1866. How LONG did it take other scientists to finally notice his work?
questions.answer: About 34 years, after he had died
choices: About 34 years, after he had died
About one week from the printing
About two months in the same year
About 200 years after his death
questions.context: Mendel's 1866 paper was published in a small local journal and ignored. He died in 1884 still unknown. In 1900, three scientists working separately (de Vries, Correns, Tschermak) rediscovered his rules. Today he is called the father of genetics.

questions.question: Today we know the 'instructions' Mendel was tracking sit inside almost every cell. What are those instructions written in?
questions.answer: DNA, the double-helix molecule
choices: DNA, the double-helix molecule
Salt, found in every kitchen
Sugar, found in every kitchen
Iron, found in every magnet
questions.context: Mendel didn't know about DNA. The molecule was named in 1869 by Friedrich Miescher; its double-helix structure was found in 1953. But the 'units' Mendel proposed are what we now call GENES, made of DNA. His math and the chemistry matched perfectly.

questions.question: In the 1860s French scientist Louis Pasteur showed wine and milk go bad because of TINY LIVING things. What do we call them today?
questions.answer: Germs, also called microbes
choices: Germs, also called microbes
Tiny invisible flying fairies
Bits of broken glass dust
Tiny iron filings in the food
questions.context: Pasteur's experiments helped prove the 'germ theory of disease' — that infections are caused by microorganisms. Before this, many thought disease came from bad air ('miasma') or imbalanced body fluids. Pasteur showed the invisible enemy was a living thing.

questions.question: Pasteur showed you can heat milk just enough to KILL germs without ruining the taste, so it lasts longer. What is that process called today?
questions.answer: Pasteurization, named after Pasteur
choices: Pasteurization, named after Pasteur
Boiling, the simplest way to heat
Salting, the old way to preserve
Freezing, the cold way to preserve
questions.context: Pasteurization heats milk (or other liquids) just enough to kill harmful germs while keeping flavor and most nutrients. Modern milk is usually pasteurized at 72 C for 15 seconds. It saves countless children from food-borne diseases every year.

questions.question: Pasteur's swan-neck flasks of broth stayed fresh even with air flowing in. What did this experiment PROVE?
questions.answer: Life does not arise from non-life on its own
choices: Life does not arise from non-life on its own
Curved glass is bad for the taste of broth
All broths in his time were unsafe to drink
Swans were proven to be very clever birds
questions.context: Many people in Pasteur's day still believed in 'spontaneous generation' — that maggots arose from old meat. His swan-neck flasks let air in but kept dust and germs out. The broth stayed clear forever. Some of his original flasks are still preserved today.

questions.question: In 1885 Pasteur saved a 9-year-old boy named Joseph Meister who had been badly bitten by a rabid dog. How did he save the boy?
questions.answer: Gave him a brand-new rabies vaccine
choices: Gave him a brand-new rabies vaccine
Sent him to the seaside for fresh air
Wrapped his arm in a special bandage
Told him not to drink any water at all
questions.context: Pasteur's rabies vaccine (1885) was risky — rabies is almost 100% fatal once symptoms appear. The vaccine worked, and Meister lived to be an adult. He later worked as a gatekeeper at the Pasteur Institute.

questions.question: In 1953 two young scientists in England figured out the shape of DNA. The famous shape looks like a twisted ladder. What's it called?
questions.answer: A double helix, like a twisted ladder
choices: A double helix, like a twisted ladder
A single loop, just one curved circle
A flat square, like a small window
A flat sheet, like a piece of paper
questions.context: DNA's double helix is made of two strands wound around each other. Each strand is built from four letters (A, T, G, C). Watson and Crick announced the shape in 1953 at the Eagle Pub in Cambridge. Their one-page paper was published in Nature on April 25, 1953.

questions.question: Watson and Crick's DNA shape was helped by an X-ray photo taken by chemist Rosalind Franklin. What was that famous picture called?
questions.answer: Photo 51, an X-ray of DNA
choices: Photo 51, an X-ray of DNA
The Big Picture, of all chemistry
Photo Helix, of a clear test tube
The Spiral Snapshot, of a glass slide
questions.context: Rosalind Franklin and her PhD student Raymond Gosling took Photo 51 in 1952 — an X-ray showing DNA's helical pattern. Watson saw the photo without Franklin's knowledge. She died of cancer in 1958 at age 37. Watson, Crick, and Wilkins won the Nobel in 1962.

questions.question: DNA is found inside almost every cell of every living thing. What does DNA actually carry?
questions.answer: Instructions for building living things
choices: Instructions for building living things
Tiny pictures of each memory you have
Stored sunlight from earlier in the day
Pure water in a very thin liquid form
questions.context: DNA carries the genetic code — instructions for making everything in a living thing, from eye color to how a leaf grows. The code is written with four letters (A, T, G, C) in long sequences called genes. Humans share about 99.9% of their DNA with each other.

questions.question: DNA's two strands can unzip, and each one makes a perfect new copy of itself. What does this let cells do?
questions.answer: Copy themselves, so bodies can grow
choices: Copy themselves, so bodies can grow
Stop growing once a baby is born safely
Float out of the body each spring
Glow brightly in the dark at night
questions.context: Each strand of DNA's double helix is a 'template' — when the strands unzip, each side serves as a master for building its missing half. This is how a single fertilized egg can become a whole baby with trillions of cells, all carrying identical DNA.

questions.question: Doctors said ulcers came from stress and spicy food. In 1984 Barry Marshall did something SHOCKING to prove it was a germ. What?
questions.answer: He drank a glass of the ulcer germ himself
choices: He drank a glass of the ulcer germ himself
He sent a sample of it to outer space
He spread it on a wall to see it grow
He let his pet dog drink it instead
questions.context: Marshall and Robin Warren had identified Helicobacter pylori in ulcer patients. Other doctors didn't believe a germ could survive stomach acid. Marshall drank a beaker of it, developed stomach inflammation in days, then cured himself with antibiotics.

questions.question: After Barry Marshall drank the ulcer germ and PROVED his theory, what happened to him in later years?
questions.answer: He won the Nobel Prize for that discovery
choices: He won the Nobel Prize for that discovery
He was sent to jail for unsafe testing
He vanished and was never seen again
He lost his medical license forever
questions.context: Marshall developed gastritis within days of drinking H. pylori, exactly as his theory predicted. He cured himself with antibiotics. Ulcers are now routinely treated as a bacterial infection. In 2005 he and Robin Warren shared the Nobel Prize in Medicine.

questions.question: Marshall's story shows medical 'common knowledge' was wrong for decades. What's the lesson for kids?
questions.answer: It is okay to ask 'how do we KNOW that?'
choices: It is okay to ask 'how do we KNOW that?'
All doctors agree on every question always
Spicy food actually does cause ulcers
Outsiders are usually wrong about hidden truths
questions.context: Marshall's story is now taught in medical schools. Real science is open to questioning, even when an answer is repeated in every textbook. The opposite of science is 'because I said so.' Honest doubt is a core virtue.

questions.question: A kid sees mold on bread in the dark drawer but not on bread in sunlight, and wonders if sun slows mold. What is that called?
questions.answer: An observation leading to a question
choices: An observation leading to a question
A finished proof of how mold grows
A guess about future weather changes
A list of every food in the house
questions.context: Science usually starts with NOTICING something and ASKING WHY. From that question, a scientist makes a guess (a hypothesis) and tries to test it. Big ideas often start with quiet, careful noticing.

questions.question: A scientist guesses, 'Salt makes ice melt faster.' She plans an experiment to check. What is this kind of testable guess called?
questions.answer: A hypothesis, a testable scientific guess
choices: A hypothesis, a testable scientific guess
A theorem, a proved math statement
A poem, a piece of written art
A fact, something already proven true
questions.context: A hypothesis is a specific testable guess — not just a hope. A good hypothesis CAN be proved wrong by an experiment. After many tests support a hypothesis, it can grow into a 'theory.'

questions.question: A team thinks plants grow taller with music. One plant gets music; one gets nothing. The 'no music' plant has a special name. What is it?
questions.answer: The control, used to compare results
choices: The control, used to compare results
The cheater, to make answers fit
The mistake, that should not be there
The boss, watching the other plant
questions.context: A control is the sample that gets the normal treatment, so you can compare. Without a control, you can't tell if music caused any difference or if it would have happened anyway. Good experiments always have a control group.

questions.question: Sasha tries her ice-melting idea once. Then she tries it 20 more times. WHY does a good scientist repeat an experiment?
questions.answer: A single try might be a lucky fluke
choices: A single try might be a lucky fluke
Repeats make the answer come out any way
The first try never counts in any case
Scientists run out of things to do anyway
questions.context: REPLICATION (repeating the experiment) is one of the most important rules in science. A single result might be luck. Strong patterns hold up across many tries. When results DON'T replicate, that's important too: the first finding might be wrong.

questions.question: A scientist's experiment shows her favorite idea is WRONG. What is the honest thing for her to do?
questions.answer: Admit it, even if she wanted to be right
choices: Admit it, even if she wanted to be right
Hide the result and stick with her favorite
Change the data to make her idea fit
Never tell anyone what really happened
questions.context: Admitting when you were WRONG is one of the hardest and most important parts of science. Many famous scientists (Einstein, Linus Pauling) had ideas that turned out to be wrong. Hiding bad results is fraud and can ruin a career.

questions.question: Why is it good for scientists to SHARE their experiments so other people can repeat them?
questions.answer: Others can spot mistakes and check the result
choices: Others can spot mistakes and check the result
Sharing makes the scientist many friends
Sharing is just being nice, not about truth
It keeps the experiment a family secret
questions.context: Science depends on OPEN sharing. When experiments are kept secret, errors and even fraud can hide for a long time. Shared experiments can be repeated and checked. This is the heart of why science usually self-corrects over time.

questions.question: Old doctors said worms appeared in rotting meat by themselves. Pasteur's experiments proved them WRONG. What is the lesson?
questions.answer: Science updates with better evidence
choices: Science updates with better evidence
All very old ideas are still correct today
Pasteur was secretly only joking around
Doctors should never change their minds
questions.context: 'Spontaneous generation' (life arising from non-life like rotting meat) was believed for centuries. Pasteur's swan-neck-flask experiments in the 1860s disproved it for good. Real science follows the evidence, even when it's uncomfortable for old beliefs.

questions.question: An honest scientist sometimes says, 'I don't know yet.' Is that okay?
questions.answer: Yes, sometimes the truthful answer is unknown
choices: Yes, sometimes the truthful answer is unknown
No, scientists are supposed to know everything
No, scientists who say it lose their careers
Yes, but only if no one else is listening
questions.context: There are still many open mysteries — what dark matter is, how life first started, how consciousness works. Pretending to know when you don't is worse than admitting it. 'I don't know — let's find out' is the spirit of real science.

questions.question: A scientist writes down only the numbers that match her favorite idea. She throws OUT the other numbers. Is this okay?
questions.answer: No, hiding data is a form of cheating
choices: No, hiding data is a form of cheating
Yes, only the good numbers really matter
Yes, this is normal everyday science work
Only if the good numbers are much bigger
questions.context: Throwing out data you don't like is called 'cherry-picking' and it is a form of scientific fraud. ALL data matters. Honest scientists report results that contradicted their hopes, too. Scientific notebooks are kept so others can see all the data.

questions.question: Old stories like 'Earth is flat' or 'ulcers from stress' end the same way: better evidence wins. The GOOD lesson?
questions.answer: Science fixes its own mistakes over time
choices: Science fixes its own mistakes over time
Old beliefs are always right; nothing changes
Smart people in the past made no mistakes
Only modern people can ever be correct
questions.context: Science is special because of its built-in habit of self-correction: open inquiry, sharing data, testing claims, replication, and the willingness to admit when an old answer was wrong. It doesn't always work fast — Galileo waited centuries for an apology. But it works.

questions.question: In 1928 Alexander Fleming came back to his messy London lab and saw a mold killing germs on a dirty dish. What did this become?
questions.answer: Penicillin, the first true antibiotic
choices: Penicillin, the first true antibiotic
A new kind of cleaning soap for labs
A medicine to help bald hair grow back
A glue used to repair broken pieces
questions.context: Fleming noticed Penicillium mold killed bacteria on a contaminated petri dish. He published the find in 1929. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford figured out how to mass-produce it in the early 1940s. By D-Day 1944 penicillin was saving Allied soldiers. Fleming, Florey, and Chain shared the 1945 Nobel.

questions.question: President Franklin D. Roosevelt couldn't walk because of a disease he caught at 39. Which disease scared US families every summer back then?
questions.answer: Polio, the summer paralysis disease
choices: Polio, the summer paralysis disease
Smallpox, the deadly old plague
Measles, the spotted rash disease
Chickenpox, with itchy red blisters
questions.context: FDR was paralyzed by polio in 1921 at age 39 and used a wheelchair for the rest of his life (mostly hidden from the public). He started the March of Dimes in 1938 to fund a cure. That research helped pay for Jonas Salk's work, which gave a vaccine in 1955 — 10 years after FDR's death.

questions.question: Alfred Wegener said the continents had once been joined and slowly DRIFTED apart. How did most scientists FIRST react?
questions.answer: Laughed and rejected it for about 50 years
choices: Laughed and rejected it for about 50 years
Believed him right away and built a statue
Sent him a Nobel Prize within a month
Welcomed his idea instantly across Europe
questions.context: Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912. He noted South America and Africa look like they fit together, plus matching fossils and rocks on both sides. Geologists rejected it because he had no MECHANISM. In the 1960s, seafloor spreading proved him right — but he had died on an Arctic expedition in 1930.
